Review: “Bayesian Semi-Blind Deconvolution at
Scale”
September 15, 2026
1 Summary
This manuscript focuses on a Bayesian model for semi-blind de-convolution
described in Senn et al. (2025). This is a challenging task where not only the
true image is unknown but also the convolution filter. By exploiting conjugacy
relations between the various prior and likelihood components, together with
the focus on cyclic lattices, the posterior can be efficiently explored through a
Gibbs sampler that relies heavily on the use of the fast Fourier transform (FFT)
and its inverse (IFFT).
From the computational perspective, this manuscript presents two improve-
ments over Senn et al. (2025): an increased use of the FFT, and an alternative
update of the blur that uses a marginal conditional instead of the usual full
conditional. According to the experimental results, there is some evidence that
the marginal version helps in dealing with multimodality issues that arise when
there is little data available.
While I think the subject of the manuscript is interesting and relevant to
JCGS, in my opinion the two improvements described above are not important
enough to justify publishing a new paper. I expand on this and other issues in
the following comments. Excerpts from the manuscript are emphasized.
2 Major comments
As I mentioned above, the main issue with this manuscript is the lack of
substantial work that is not already found in Senn et al. (2025). A side-by-side
comparison shows that almost everything in the paper up to Section 4.1 can
be found in the 2025 paper (Section 4.2 describes the marginal HMC sampler
which is new). If there are new contributions up to Section 4.1, they are hard to
detect because the bulk of the text is dedicated to explaining things that are
already in Senn et al. (2025). A new version of the present manuscript should
avoid repetition of previous work as much as possible, and anything that must
be included should be placed in Section 2 (preliminaries) so that readers can
clearly distinguish the novel contributions from past work. Moreover, a new
1
version should at the very least attempt a more thorough empirical examination
of the pros and cons of the two competing samplers.
On a more technical note, I think there may be a theoretical problem with the
way the Gaussian field is defined on the cyclic lattice. Following Borovitskiy et al.
(2020), the so-called naive generalization of a Gaussian process in Euclidean
space to a compact manifold, where the Euclidean norm is simply substituted
with the geodesic distance, does not yield a positive definite kernel. But this is
precisely what Senn et al. (2025) and the present manuscript do to build the
Gaussian field on the flat torus (i.e., the cyclic lattice). In a practical numerical
implementation, this would show up as negative eigenvalues that need to be
truncated to 0 in order to avoid taking the square root of a negative number
(see line 2 in Algorithm 2 of the manuscript).
Interestingly, Borovitskiy et al. (2020) show that for the flat torus, the
naive generalization is correct to a first order approximation, which means that
for short length scales and/or large embedding grids the resulting covariance
matrices may be positive definite. This is the same phenomenon that underlies
the circulant embedding technique for sampling general stationary Gaussian
random fields (Graham et al., 2018). Thus, when the authors justify the use of
an embedding lattice to remove boundary effects, they should also mention that
a larger embedding is needed to handle non-definiteness issues that may show
with sufficiently large length scales.
An alternative that completely elides the non-definiteness issue is to work
with the conditional autoregressive model CAR( ρ,σ 2) with ρ∈ [0, 1), which
yields positive definite precision—and thus covariance—matrices regardless of
the graph being considered (Gelfand and Vounatsou, 2003, Section 3).
3 Minor comments
Section 1
Comment 1: P.1 L9–10: “...reflectivity image, well reflectivity, noise and
seismic wavelet...” . These terms are not known in the statistical community.
They should first be explained before being discussed.
Comment 2: P.4 L50–51: book citations need to include a pointer to the
section that contains the claim; e.g., (Liu, 2008, Section X.Y.Z). This happens
multiple times in the manuscript, with Liu’s book but also with Davis’ and Rue
& Held.
Section 2
Comment 3: P.5 L39–40: using p(x) to denote the density of a parametrized
family like Nn(µ, Σ) is bad practice, because there are multiple dimensions,
means, and covariance parameters considered in this study. For example, a fairly
2
common approach is to write Nn(x;µ, Σ) for such a density; many other options
are possible.
Comment 4: P.5 L46–49: consider adding a citation for these formulas or a
short proof. I think that statisticians are more aware of the case of a multivariate
normal vector z = (z1,z 2) and the conditional distribution of z2 given z1 is
conditioned on either of its components (see e.g. Mardia et al., 1979, Thm 3.2.4),
which in turn can be used to get Eq (3).
Comment 5: P.5 L56–57: the error does not enter the formula for the covari-
ance matrix so the value of the error cannot affect the rank.
Comment 6: P.6 L15–16: cite Rue and Held (2005, Section 2.3.3)
Comment 7: Eq 7: The matrices Fn and F H
n are interchanged; see Davis
(1979, Eq. 3.2.7). Also happens in P.8 L14–15.
Comment 8: P. 8 L45–46: formula for the mn eigenvalues is wrong, should
be λC =√mn (Fm⊗Fn)Hvec(Π).
Comment 9: Algorithm 2: this is essentially Algorithm 2.10 in Rue and Held
(2005), cite it. Note that page 65 of that book states clearly that the assumption
is that the precision (and thus the covariance) matrix is symmetric positive
definite.
Section 3
Comment 10: Most of this section is from Senn et al. (2025), so it should go
in Section 2 if absolutely necessary.
Section 4
Comment 11: Section 4.1 is mostly all in Senn et al. (2025), so it should be
placed in Section 2 if absolutely necessary.
Section 5
Comment 12: Figure 2: I think this figure is nice but it doesn’t quite convey
the message that the HMC version is better at handling the multimodality. It
would be nice have another plot that focused only on the most volatile index of
the blur vector so that a traditional histogram could be shown. A sampler that
truly overcomes the multimodality issue would have roughly half of its samples
on each mode. This fact cannot be easily assessed from Fig 2.
Comment 13: P. 28 L21–22: typo, should be “lattice”.
3
Comment 14: Section 5.2: Would it be possible to do a similar analysis as in
the previous section where some of the exact observations are withheld? This
would help showcase the benefits of the HMC version.
